claims.claim: Young honeybees perform numerous inside tasks, most prominently brood care in form of alloparental nursing behavior, before transitioning to other in-hive tasks.
claims.source: Young bees perform numerous inside tasks, most prominently brood care in form of alloparental nursing behavior, before transitioning to a mix of other in-hive tasks (Johnson, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Older honeybees as outside foragers are almost exclusive of other tasks.
claims.source: Similar to the highly specialized nursing stage, the final behavioral state of older bees as outside foragers is almost exclusive of other tasks (Seeley, 1982).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Honeybee foragers often specialize on collecting only one of the principal food sources, pollen or nectar.
claims.source: Moreover, foragers often specialize on collecting only one of the principal food sources, pollen or nectar (Page et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Specialized nurse bees, nectar foragers, and pollen foragers are also found in Apis cerana.
claims.source: Specialized nurse bees (NBs), nectar foragers (NFs), and pollen foragers (PFs) are also found in the closely related Eastern honeybee, Apis cerana (Ji et al., 2020), thus offering a suitable parallel system for our study.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Responsiveness to brood pheromones peaks at typical nursing age.
claims.source: Responsiveness to brood pheromones peaks at typical nursing age (Pankiw, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Foragers have a lower response threshold to sugars and light than nurses.
claims.source: In contrast, foragers have a lower response threshold to sugars and light than nurses (Değirmenci et al., 2018; Ben-Shahar et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Among foragers, pollen specialists exhibit higher responsiveness to sucrose and pollen stimuli than nectar foragers.
claims.source: Among foragers, pollen specialists exhibit higher responsiveness to sucrose and pollen stimuli than NFs (Page et al., 1998; Pankiw and Page, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Response thresholds can be modified by biogenic amines including dopamine, 5-hydroxy-tryptamine, octopamine, and tyramine.
claims.source: Response thresholds can be modified by biogenic amines, and dopamine, 5-hydroxy-tryptamine, octopamine, and tyramine have been implicated in the regulation of different behaviors of worker bees although the mechanisms are not entirely clear (Schulz et al., 2002; Scheiner et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Neuropeptides are a diverse group of neurotransmitters that can also act as neurohormones on distal targets to coordinate a wide range of internal states and behavioral processes.
claims.source: Few studies have addressed the role of neuropeptides although they are a diverse group of neurotransmitters that can also act as neurohormones on distal targets to coordinate a wide range of internal states and behavioral processes (Nässel, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Neuropeptides are intimately involved in food perception and social interaction of insects.
claims.source: Neuropeptides are intimately involved in food perception and social interaction of insects (Schoofs et al., 2017), two processes that are central to division of labor in social insects (Ament et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Neuropeptides mediate pheromonal effects on physiology.
claims.source: Neuropeptides mediate pheromonal effects on physiology (Shankar et al., 2015; Gendron et al., 2014) and usually exhibit a high degree of specificity (Inagaki et al., 2014; Taghert and Nitabach, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Neuropeptides usually exhibit a high degree of specificity.
claims.source: Neuropeptides mediate pheromonal effects on physiology (Shankar et al., 2015; Gendron et al., 2014) and usually exhibit a high degree of specificity (Inagaki et al., 2014; Taghert and Nitabach, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Neuropeptides have been implicated in honeybee worker specialization and division of labor.
claims.source: Therefore, neuropeptides are prime candidates for mediating the independent adjustment of socially relevant response thresholds and they have been implicated in honeybee worker specialization and division of labor (Ji et al., 2020; Brockmann et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: More than 100 mature neuropeptides derived from 22 protein precursors have been identified in Apis mellifera.
claims.source: More than 100 mature neuropeptides derived from 22 protein precursors have been identified in the Western honeybee, A. mellifera (Han et al., 2015; Boerjan et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Several neuropeptides, including allatostatin, leucokinin, and tachykinin-related peptides, may be involved in the control of social behavior of A. mellifera and A. cerana.
claims.source: Several neuropeptides, including allatostatin, leucokinin, and tachykinin-related peptides (TRPs), may be involved in the control of social behavior of A. mellifera and the closely related A. cerana, such as aggression (Pratavieira et al., 2018), foraging (Ji et al., 2020; Brockmann et al., 2009), brood care (Han et al., 2015), and possibly a wide array of other behaviors (Pratavieira et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The proportion of pollen foragers showing a PER increased with increasing concentrations of sucrose solutions in both Apis mellifera ligustica and Apis cerana cerana.
claims.source: The percentage of bees showing a PER increased with sucrose concentration across all experimental groups (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: In both AML and ACC, the sucrose response scores of pollen foragers were higher than the SRSs of nectar foragers.
claims.source: In both, Apis mellifera ligustica (AML) and Apis cerana cerana (ACC), the sucrose response scores (SRSs) of PFs were higher than the SRSs of NFs (AML: Z = 7.0, p≤0.001; ACC: Z = 6.1, p<0.001)
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In both AML and ACC, the sucrose response scores of pollen foragers were higher than the SRSs of nurse bees.
claims.source: In both, Apis mellifera ligustica (AML) and Apis cerana cerana (ACC), the sucrose response scores (SRSs) of PFs were higher than the SRSs of NFs (AML: Z = 7.0, p≤0.001; ACC: Z = 6.1, p<0.001) and nurse bees (NBs) (AML: Z = 5.9, p<0.001; ACC: Z = 5.2, p<0.001)
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: No significant difference between nectar foragers and nurse bees was observed in either AML or ACC species.
claims.source: while no significant difference between NFs and NBs was observed in either species (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Pollen foragers of AML showed significantly higher sucrose responsiveness than pollen foragers of ACC.
claims.source: The species comparison between AML and ACC showed significant higher sucrose responsiveness in PFs of AML than in PFs of ACC (Z = 2.361, p=0.018), specifically at sucrose concentrations of 0.3% (χ2 = 4.1, p=0.042), 1.0% (χ2 = 5.2, p=0.001), 3.0% (χ2 = 8.4, p=0.023), and 10.0% (χ2 = 5.3, p=0.021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Nectar foragers of AML and ACC showed no significant difference in overall SRS.
claims.source: NFs of AML and ACC showed no significant difference in overall SRS, but NFs of AML were more responsive than NFs of ACC at sucrose concentrations of 0.3% (χ2 = 4.5, p=0.035), 1.0% (χ2 = 4.5, p=0.033), and 3.0% (χ2 = 4.0, p=0.046).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference between nurse bees of AML and ACC in sucrose responsiveness.
claims.source: There was no significant difference between NBs of AML and ACC in sucrose responsiveness.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In AML, pollen foragers were more responsive to pollen stimulation than nectar foragers.
claims.source: In AML, PFs were more responsive to pollen stimulation than NFs (χ2 = 14.9, p=0.002) and NBs (χ2 = 20.2, p<0.001), while there were no significantly statistical differences between NFs and NBs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In AML, pollen foragers were more responsive to pollen stimulation than nurse bees.
claims.source: In AML, PFs were more responsive to pollen stimulation than NFs (χ2 = 14.9, p=0.002) and NBs (χ2 = 20.2, p<0.001), while there were no significantly statistical differences between NFs and NBs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In ACC, pollen foragers were more sensitive to pollen than nectar foragers.
claims.source: Likewise, PFs of ACC were more sensitive than NFs (χ2 = 6.0, p=0.015) and NBs (χ2 = 7.8, p=0.001) without a statistically significant difference between NFs and NBs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In ACC, pollen foragers were more sensitive to pollen than nurse bees.
claims.source: Likewise, PFs of ACC were more sensitive than NFs (χ2 = 6.0, p=0.015) and NBs (χ2 = 7.8, p=0.001) without a statistically significant difference between NFs and NBs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Pollen foragers of AML showed a significant higher pollen responsiveness than pollen foragers of ACC.
claims.source: PFs of AML showed a significant higher pollen responsiveness than of ACC (χ2 = 4.9, p=0.031), with no significant species differences in NFs and NBs (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Nurse bees of AML showed increased responsiveness to larva stimulation compared to pollen foragers.
claims.source: In larva responsiveness assay, NBs of AML showed increased responsiveness to larva stimulation compared to PFs (χ2 = 7.2, p=0.006) and NFs (χ2 = 10.3, p=0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Nurse bees of AML showed increased responsiveness to larva stimulation compared to nectar foragers.
claims.source: In larva responsiveness assay, NBs of AML showed increased responsiveness to larva stimulation compared to PFs (χ2 = 7.2, p=0.006) and NFs (χ2 = 10.3, p=0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Nurse bees of ACC were more sensitive to larvae than pollen foragers.
claims.source: Likewise, NBs of ACC were more sensitive than PFs (χ2 = 4.2, p=0.013) and NFs (χ2 = 6.1, p=0.002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Nurse bees of ACC were more sensitive to larvae than nectar foragers.
claims.source: Likewise, NBs of ACC were more sensitive than PFs (χ2 = 4.2, p=0.013) and NFs (χ2 = 6.1, p=0.002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Nurse bees of AML were significantly more sensitive to larvae than nurse bees of ACC.
claims.source: NBs of AML were significantly more sensitive to larvae (χ2 = 4.3, p=0.027) than NBs of ACC, with no significant species differences in PFs and NFs (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Behavioral specialization among the workers of both honeybee species correspond to differences in the workers' responsiveness to task-relevant stimuli.
claims.source: In sum, our results indicated that behavioral specialization among the workers of both honeybee species correspond to differences in the workers' responsiveness to task-relevant stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claims.claim: 132 unique neuropeptides derived from 23 neuropeptide families were identified in the brain of AML worker bees.
claims.source: Overall, 132 unique neuropeptides derived from 23 neuropeptide families were identified in the brain of AML worker bees (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claims.claim: 116 unique neuropeptides derived from 22 neuropeptide families were identified in the brain of ACC worker bees.
claims.source: In the brain of ACC worker bees, 116 unique neuropeptides derived from 22 neuropeptide families were identified (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data analysis.

claims.claim: 40 neuropeptides derived from 16 neuropeptide families were differentially expressed in the brain among the three behavioral phenotypes of AML.
claims.source: Quantitative comparison among the three behavioral phenotypes of AML showed that 40 neuropeptides derived from 16 neuropeptide families were differentially expressed the brain (Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative neuropeptidomics data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Only TRP2 and TRP3 showed consistent patterns relating to the task-specific responsiveness of the experimental groups.
claims.source: The comparisons revealed numerous differences among experimental groups, but only two tachykinin-related peptides (TRP2 and TRP3) showed consistent patterns relating to the task-specific responsiveness of the experimental groups.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the neuropeptidomics data across both species and all behavioral phenotypes.

claims.claim: Consistent differences between NBs, NFs, and PFs of both species were only found for TRP2 and TRP3.
claims.source: Thus, this global comparison of brain neuropeptide levels revealed numerous quantitative and qualitative differences. However, consistent differences between NBs, NFs, and PFs of both species were only found for TRP2 and TRP3, prompting their further study.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of neuropeptidomics data.

claims.claim: Injection of TRP2 peptide significantly reduced the SRS of pollen foragers.
claims.source: Injection of the TRP2 peptide significantly reduced the SRS of PFs (Z = 2.2, p=0.031), significantly reducing PER responses to all sucrose concentrations used.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from TRP2 injection experiments.

claims.claim: Nectar foragers injected with TRP2 displayed significantly lower SRS than control-injected nectar foragers.
claims.source: Similarly, NFs injected with TRP2 displayed significantly lower SRS than control-injected NFs (Z = 2.3, p=0.019), significantly reducing PER responses to all sucrose concentrations except 0.1% (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from TRP2 injection experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: TRP2-injected nurse bees did not show significant responsiveness changes to sucrose relative to controls.
claims.source: In contrast, TRP2-injected NBs did not show significant responsiveness changes to sucrose relative to controls.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from TRP2 injection experiments.

claims.claim: Pollen foragers showed significantly decreased responsiveness to pollen loads after TRP2 injection.
claims.source: For pollen stimulation, PFs showed significantly decreased responsiveness to pollen loads after TRP2 injection (χ2 = 6.7, p=0.017), while no significant effects were observed in PFs and NFs (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from TRP2 injection experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Injection of TRP2 only significantly affected the responsiveness of nurse bees to larvae but not nectar foragers or pollen foragers.
claims.source: In the larval responsiveness assay, injection of TRP2 only significantly affected the responsiveness of NBs (χ2 = 6.1, p=0.001) but not NFs or PFs (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from TRP2 injection experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Knockdown efficiencies were close to 60% for TRP and TRPR mRNA levels at 24 hr post-injection of the corresponding dsRNA.
claims.source: Knockdown efficiencies were close to 60% for TRP and TRPR mRNA levels at 24 hr post-injection of the corresponding dsRNA (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data measuring knockdown efficiency.

claims.claim: Knockdown of either TRP or TRPR significantly increased the SRS of nectar foragers.
claims.source: Relative to control injections, knockdown of either TRP or TRPR significantly increased the SRS of NFs (dsTRP: Z = 2.4, p=0.049; dsTRPR: Z = 2.6, p=0.025)
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Knockdown of TRP and TRPR did not significantly change the overall SRS of pollen foragers and nurse bees.
claims.source: Knockdown of TRP and TRPR did not significantly change the overall SRS of PFs and NBs, although it significantly increased the responses of PFs to sucrose at concentrations of 0.1% (dsTRP: χ2 = 4.4, p=0.029; dsTRPR: χ2 = 6.1, p=0.011), 0.3% (dsTRP: χ2 = 5.2, p=0.018; dsTRPR: χ2 = 6.0, p=0.011), and 1.0% (dsTRP: χ2 = 5.0, p=0.020; dsTRPR: χ2 = 4.7, p=0.025).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Knockdown of either TRP or TRPR specifically increased the pollen responsiveness of pollen foragers.
claims.source: Responses to pollen stimulation after dsRNA injection indicated that knockdown of either TRP or TRPR specifically increased the pollen responsiveness of PFs (dsTRP: χ2 = 6.5, p=0.018; dsTRPR: χ2 = 6.4, p=0.010), whereas the effects on NFs and NBs were not significant (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The responsiveness of nurse bees to larvae was significantly increased after gene knockdown of either TRP or TRPR.
claims.source: The responsiveness of NBs to larvae was significantly increased after gene knockdown of either TRP (χ2 = 4.4, p=0.029) or TRPR (χ2 = 4.8, p=0.023), but NFs and PFs were not affected (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNAi knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: TRP signaling generally regulates the degree of behavioral specialization by moderating the responsiveness to task-specific stimuli in behavioral specialists.
claims.source: The experimental up- and downregulation of TRP signaling resulted in complementary changes in the responsiveness of our experimental groups in a specific way: Only the particular, increased responsiveness to task-relevant stimuli of each behavioral group was affected, suggesting that TRP signaling generally regulates the degree of behavioral specialization by moderating the responsiveness to task-specific stimuli in behavioral specialists.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined results of TRP2 injection and RNAi knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: The honeybee TRPR was exclusively localized in the cell membrane.
claims.source: Significant cell surface expression was observed by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1), revealing that the honeybee TRPR was exclusively localized in the cell membrane.
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Competitive binding assays confirmed the predicted high affinity of the TRPR for both TRP2 and TRP3.
claims.source: Competitive binding assays with labeled TRP2 and TRP3 confirmed the predicted high affinity of the TRPR for both, although it was higher for TRP2 than for TRP3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by competitive binding assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: TRPR has higher affinity for TRP2 than for TRP3.
claims.source: Competitive binding assays with labeled TRP2 and TRP3 confirmed the predicted high affinity of the TRPR for both, although it was higher for TRP2 than for TRP3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by competitive binding assay data.

claims.claim: TRP2 and TRP3 can activate TRPR and trigger cAMP signaling.
claims.source: The detected accumulation of intracellular cAMP concentration only in HEK293 cells transformed with TRPR (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 2) confirmed that TRP2 and TRP3 can activate TRPR and trigger cAMP signaling.
claims.evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Selective inhibition/activation experiments implicated the Gαs and Gαq (but not Gαi) subunits in TRP/TRPR signaling mechanism.
claims.source: Correspondingly, selective inhibition/activation experiments implicated the Gαs and Gαq (but not Gαi) subunits in this signaling mechanism (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Figure 5—source data 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments using specific inhibitors and activators shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Intracellular Ca2+ mobilization resulted from TRP2 or TRP3 stimulation, dependent on Gαq.
claims.source: Furthermore, intracellular Ca2+ mobilization was also found to result from TRP2 or TRP3 stimulation, dependent on Gαq (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 4, and Figure 5—source data 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Treatment with different concentrations of TRP2 induced a transient, dose-dependent phosphorylation of ERK in both HEK293 and Sf21 cells.
claims.source: Treatment with different concentrations of TRP2 induced a transient, dose-dependent phosphorylation of ERK in both HEK293 (EC50 = 68.04 nM) and Sf21 (EC50 = 1.68 nM) cells (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 5, Figure 5—source data 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: TRP2 elicited transient phosphorylation of ERK with maximal phosphorylation at 2 min and near basal levels by 90 min.
claims.source: Further time-dependent analysis indicated that TRP2 elicited transient phosphorylation of ERK with maximal phosphorylation at 2 min and near basal levels by 90 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 5, Figure 5—source data 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by time-course Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Honeybee TRP/TRPR signaling dually coupled to Gαs and Gαq proteins to activate the ERK signaling pathway.
claims.source: Treatment with MEK inhibitor U0126, PKA inhibitor H89, and PKC inhibitor Go6983, respectively, led to a significant inhibition of TRP/TRPR-mediated ERK activation, whereas Gαi inhibitor pertussis toxin (PTX) had no effect, demonstrating that honeybee TRP/TRPR signaling dually coupled to Gαs and Gαq proteins to activate the ERK signaling pathway (Figure 5—figure supplement 5, Figure 5—source data 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments using specific inhibitors shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: The level of phosphorylated ERK significantly increased after injection of TRP2 peptide into nurse bees, pollen foragers, and nectar foragers.
claims.source: Western blot results confirmed that TRP/TRPR signaling triggers ERK signaling in vivo. The level of phosphorylated ERK significantly increased after injection of TRP2 peptide into NBs, PFs, and NFs (Figure 6A)
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data from in vivo experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The level of phosphorylated ERK decreased after knockdown of the TRP or TRPR transcripts.
claims.source: The level of phosphorylated ERK significantly increased after injection of TRP2 peptide into NBs, PFs, and NFs (Figure 6A) and decreased after knockdown of the TRP or TRPR transcripts (Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Western blot data from in vivo RNAi experiments shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Responsiveness to task-relevant stimuli correlates with behavioral specialization in two different honeybee species.
claims.source: In this study, we demonstrated that the responsiveness to task-relevant stimuli correlates with behavioral specialization in two different honeybee species.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the PER experiments presented in the Results section.

claims.claim: TRP2 and TRP3 were identified as putative mechanism to adjust task-specific response thresholds and thus proximally guide division of labor.
claims.source: Through parallel characterization of the neuropeptidome, we identified two tachykinin-related peptides (TRP2 and TRP3) as putative mechanism to adjust task-specific response thresholds and thus proximally guide division of labor.
claims.evidence: This is based on the neuropeptidomics data and subsequent functional experiments.

claims.claim: TRP2 and TRP3 bind to their membrane-bound receptor.
claims.source: Subsequently, we characterized the molecular action of TRP2 and TRP3 in cell culture by verifying their binding to their membrane-bound receptor and demonstrating activation of multiple downstream signaling mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is supported by competitive binding assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: TRP2 and TRP3 activate multiple downstream signaling mechanisms.
claims.source: Subsequently, we characterized the molecular action of TRP2 and TRP3 in cell culture by verifying their binding to their membrane-bound receptor and demonstrating activation of multiple downstream signaling mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments showing cAMP accumulation, Ca2+ mobilization, and ERK phosphorylation.

claims.claim: Injection of TRP2 decreased task-specific responses while downregulation of TRP or TRPR increased the same specific responses.
claims.source: Finally, we verified causal involvement of TRP signaling in modulating task-specific behavioral response thresholds through complementary outcomes of TRP2 injection and RNAi-mediated knockdown of TRP and TRPR: while injection decreased task-specific responses, downregulation of TRP or TRPR increased the same specific responses.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the combined results of TRP2 injection and RNAi experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claims.claim: TRP signaling tunes the behavioral responsiveness of animals to specific stimuli compared to others.
claims.source: Thus, we present a mechanism that tunes the behavioral responsiveness of animals to specific stimuli compared to others.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined experimental results.

claims.claim: The function of TRP signaling in adjusting context specificity of behavioral responses could be more widely conserved in animals.
claims.source: We use behaviorally specialized honeybee workers as models but hypothesize that this function of TRP signaling could be more widely conserved to adjust the context specificity of behavioral responses in animals.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis extending the findings to other animals.

claims.claim: Neuropeptides represent the largest and most diverse category of signaling molecules in the nervous system.
claims.source: Among all the signaling molecules in the nervous system, neuropeptides represent the largest and most diverse category and are crucial in orchestrating various biological processes and behavioral actions (Burbach, 2011; Hökfelt et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: TRPs have been associated with the modulation of appetitive olfactory sensation.
claims.source: TRPs have been associated with the modulation of appetitive olfactory sensation (Ki et al., 2015; Winther et al., 2006; Gui et al., 2017), foraging (Pratavieira et al., 2018), sex pheromone perception (Shankar et al., 2015), and aggression (Asahina et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: TRP is preferentially expressed in the mushroom body and some neurons scattered in the antennal and optic lobes in honeybees.
claims.source: Particularly in honeybees, TRP is preferentially expressed in the mushroom body and some neurons scattered in the antennal and optic lobes (Takeuchi et al., 2004), and some expression has also been found in antennae (Jain and Brockmann, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Global TRP expression in the honeybee worker brain increases during the transition from nursing to foraging.
claims.source: Global TRP expression in the honeybee worker brain also increases during the transition from nursing to foraging, further implicating it in the regulation of honeybee social behavior (Pratavieira et al., 2014; Takeuchi et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: In both species, TRP2 and TRP3 were most abundant in the brain of nectar foragers, followed by pollen foragers, and finally nurse bees.
claims.source: In both species, TRP2 and TRP3 were most abundant in the brain of NFs, followed by PFs, and finally NBs.
claims.evidence: This is based on the quantitative neuropeptidomics data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The comparison between AML and ACC indicated higher TRP2 and TRP3 abundance in ACC in each behavioral phenotype.
claims.source: Moreover, the comparison between AML and ACC indicated higher TRP2 and TRP3 abundance in ACC in each behavioral phenotype, commensurate with the less specific PER responsiveness in ACC compared to AML.
claims.evidence: This is based on the quantitative neuropeptidomics data comparing the two species.

claims.claim: The action of most insect neuropeptides is mediated by binding to GPCRs and often involves cAMP and Ca2+ as second messengers.
claims.source: The action of most insect neuropeptides is mediated by binding to GPCRs and often involves cAMP and Ca2+ as second messengers (Hauser et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The TRPR is activated by TRPs triggering intracellular cAMP accumulation and Ca2+ mobilization in fruit flies and silkworms.
claims.source: The TRPR is activated by TRPs triggering intracellular cAMP accumulation and Ca2+ mobilization in fruit flies and silkworms (Bombyx mori) (He et al., 2014; Birse et al., 2006), while no cAMP responses were discovered in stable flies (Stomoxys calcitrans) (Poels et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: TRP2 displayed a higher affinity to TRPR and induced higher cAMP and Ca2+ signaling than TRP3.
claims.source: TRP2 displayed a higher affinity to TRPR and induced higher cAMP and Ca2+ signaling than TRP3, leading us to focus on TRP2 in the later in vivo experiments.
claims.evidence: This is based on the competitive binding assays and functional assays in cell culture.

claims.claim: Many GPCRs are able to induce mitogen-activated protein kinase cascades via cooperation of Gαs, Gαq, and Gαi signals, leading to the phosphorylation of ERK1/2.
claims.source: Many GPCRs are able to induce mitogen-activated protein kinase cascades via cooperation of Gαs, Gαq, and Gαi signals, leading to the phosphorylation of ERK1/2, which plays critical roles in diverse biological processes (Rozengurt, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Honeybees are very similar to silkworms with regard to the involvement of the Gαs/cAMP/PKA and Gαq/Ca2+/PKC signaling pathways in the regulation of TRP-induced ERK1/2 activation.
claims.source: Thus, honeybees seem to be very similar to silkworms with regard to the involvement of the Gαs/cAMP/PKA and Gαq/Ca2+/PKC signaling pathways in the regulation of TRP-induced ERK1/2 activation (He et al., 2014).

results.result: Task-specific responsiveness differs among behavioral phenotypes in both honeybee species. Pollen foragers show higher sucrose responsiveness than nectar foragers and nurse bees in both AML and ACC. Pollen foragers are more responsive to pollen than other phenotypes, and nurse bees are more responsive to larvae. AML workers show generally higher task-specific responsiveness than ACC workers.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C48 provide comprehensive behavioral data with appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis, chi-square) showing significant differences (p<0.05) among behavioral phenotypes for task-specific stimuli. Sample sizes are adequate (125-136 bees per group), and results are consistent across both species. The data directly support the response threshold model for division of labor.

results.result: Quantitative neuropeptidomics identified TRP2 and TRP3 as the only neuropeptides showing consistent patterns correlating with task-specific responsiveness across both species and all behavioral phenotypes. TRP2 and TRP3 levels were highest in nectar foragers, intermediate in pollen foragers, and lowest in nurse bees, inversely correlating with behavioral specialization.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 and C87-C88 are supported by LC-MS/MS data with appropriate statistical criteria (p<0.01, fold change ≥1.5). The identification of 132 and 116 neuropeptides in AML and ACC respectively provides comprehensive coverage. The consistent pattern of TRP2/TRP3 across species and phenotypes, while other neuropeptides showed variable patterns, provides strong correlative evidence for their role in behavioral regulation.

results.result: TRP2 injection specifically decreased task-specific responsiveness in behavioral specialists: it reduced sucrose responsiveness in pollen and nectar foragers, pollen responsiveness in pollen foragers, and larval responsiveness in nurse bees, without affecting non-task-related responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by experimental data with appropriate controls (ddH2O injection) and statistical tests showing significant effects (p<0.05). Sample sizes are adequate (52-58 per group). The specificity of effects—only affecting task-relevant stimuli for each phenotype—is a critical finding that strengthens the causal interpretation. However, the mechanism by which exogenous peptide injection achieves specificity remains unclear.

results.result: RNAi-mediated knockdown of TRP or TRPR produced opposite effects to TRP2 injection, specifically increasing task-specific responsiveness in behavioral specialists. Knockdown efficiency was ~60% at 24 hours, and effects were specific to task-relevant stimuli for each phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 provide complementary loss-of-function evidence with adequate knockdown efficiency verified by qRT-PCR. The opposite effects to TRP2 injection strengthen causal interpretation. Statistical tests are appropriate with adequate sample sizes (50-56 per group). The specificity of effects matching the gain-of-function experiments is compelling. However, 60% knockdown is moderate, and potential compensatory mechanisms are not addressed.

results.result: The honeybee TRPR is localized to the cell membrane and binds TRP2 and TRP3 with high affinity, with TRP2 showing higher affinity than TRP3.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 and C78 are supported by fluorescence microscopy showing membrane localization and competitive binding assays demonstrating specific, high-affinity binding. The use of both HEK293 and Sf21 cells provides cross-validation. However, the manuscript does not provide IC50 values for the competitive binding assays, which would strengthen quantitative interpretation.

results.result: TRP2 and TRP3 activate TRPR to trigger multiple downstream signaling pathways including cAMP accumulation and Ca2+ mobilization through Gαs and Gαq coupling (but not Gαi). TRP2 shows higher potency than TRP3 in activating these pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70, C79, and C91 are supported by luciferase assays for cAMP and Fura-2 AM assays for Ca2+, with appropriate controls and pharmacological inhibitors. The use of specific inhibitors (PTX, CTX, YM-254890, H89, U73122) provides mechanistic insight. Data are replicated in both HEK293 and Sf21 cells. The specificity controls (other neuropeptides showing no effect) strengthen the conclusions.

results.result: TRP/TRPR signaling activates ERK1/2 phosphorylation in a dose- and time-dependent manner through dual coupling to Gαs/cAMP/PKA and Gαq/Ca2+/PKC pathways, similar to silkworm signaling mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 and C93 are supported by Western blot data showing dose-dependent (EC50 values provided) and time-dependent ERK phosphorylation. The use of specific inhibitors (U0126, H89, Go6983) demonstrates pathway involvement. Three independent replicates are reported. The comparison to silkworms provides evolutionary context, though direct comparative experiments were not performed.

results.result: TRP2 injection increases ERK phosphorylation in vivo in all three behavioral phenotypes, while knockdown of TRP or TRPR decreases ERK phosphorylation, confirming the in vitro signaling pathway operates in living honeybees.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 are supported by Western blot data from honeybee brains with appropriate controls and statistical significance (p<0.05). The complementary effects of gain- and loss-of-function manipulations strengthen the conclusion. However, the manuscript does not address whether ERK phosphorylation differs among behavioral phenotypes at baseline, which would be informative for understanding the mechanism.

results.result: TRP signaling regulates the degree of task-specific responsiveness in specialized honeybee workers by modulating response thresholds in a context-specific manner, supporting the response threshold model for division of labor.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C64, C76-C77, C80-C81, C103-C104 synthesize the behavioral, peptidomic, and molecular data into a coherent mechanistic model. The convergence of correlative (neuropeptidomics), gain-of-function (TRP2 injection), and loss-of-function (RNAi) evidence provides strong support. The specificity of effects—only affecting task-relevant stimuli—is the key finding distinguishing this from general arousal or motivation effects.

results.result: TRP signaling may control context specificity of behavioral responses in animals more generally beyond honeybees.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C82, C105-C106 are speculative extrapolations beyond the data. While TRP signaling is conserved across insects and has been implicated in various behaviors in other species (cited in C84), the specific function in regulating task-specific response thresholds has only been demonstrated in honeybees. Cross-species functional studies would be required to support this broader claim.

results.result: ACC workers exhibit less task-specific responsiveness than AML workers, which may be explained by higher TRP2 and TRP3 levels in ACC across all behavioral phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C109, C111, C113 present an interesting correlation between species differences in behavior and neuropeptide levels. However, the interpretation is uncertain because: (1) the behavioral differences could reflect methodological artifacts (different pollen sources, environmental conditions); (2) the correlation is inverse to what might be expected if higher TRP levels simply increase responsiveness; (3) no functional experiments (TRP manipulation in ACC) were performed to test causality. The authors appropriately note that 'functional verification at the level of colony phenotypes will be required.'

results.result: ERK links TRP signaling to the insulin/insulin-like signaling (IIS) pathway, connecting TRP signaling to age-based division of labor and forager specialization.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 propose connections to IIS based on literature citations and the finding that ERK is activated by TRP signaling. However, this connection is speculative: (1) no experiments directly tested IIS involvement; (2) no measurements of insulin-like peptides were made; (3) the cited work on IIS and division of labor did not examine TRP signaling. While the hypothesis is plausible and well-motivated, it requires experimental validation.

results.result: Pollen and sucrose are distinct stimuli, as evidenced by differential effects of TRP manipulation on responsiveness to these stimuli across behavioral phenotypes. The PER to larvae is specific to nurses and linked to brood provisioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C102 are supported by the pattern of results showing that TRP manipulation affects pollen and sucrose responsiveness differently in pollen foragers (both affected) versus nectar foragers (only sucrose affected). This dissociation provides evidence for distinct neural pathways. The specificity of larval PER to nurses is well-documented. However, the mechanistic basis for how TRP signaling achieves this stimulus specificity remains unclear.
